newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania set for poll as parties threaten boycott.
newsitem.headline: Albania set for poll as parties threaten boycott.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Friday called early elections aimed at stopping Albania's slide to violence although most political parties were still threatening to boycott it.
Berisha set the date for June 29, as agreed with European envoy Franz Vranitzky, who earlier called on politicians to compromise to enable the election to go ahead.
Early elections were agreed in March to help pacify Albania amid rioting and violence after thousands lost their life savings in fraudulent pyramid investment schemes.
But the elections are still mired in uncertainty as most parties have threatened to boycott the vote in a row over an election law they say favours Berisha's Democratic Party.

"The president of the republic...decreed today the dissolution of the National Assembly before the end of its mandate and the holding of new parliamentary elections on Sunday June 29, 1997," Berisha's office said in a statement.
Vranitzky, ending his fifth mission to the former Stalinist state on Friday after once more failing to find cross-party consensus, urged politicians to compromise.
He seemed late on Thursday to have brokered a fresh deal to get the elections on track but most political parties later said they were again considering boycotting the poll.
"This is the reason that political dialogue in this country must continue," former Austrian chancellor Vranitzky told a news conference.
Although much calmer, Albania still sees violence and shootings every day and the whole country is subject to a curfew from nine in the evening to five in the morning.
The Socialists, the second-largest party, remain deeply distrustful of Berisha and his right-wing former ruling party.
They said a new election law, passed in the early hours of Friday after Vranitzky persuaded politicians to amend it, was not still not acceptable.
"We are unhappy with the passage of this law," said Naim Dokle, chairman of the Socialist Party parliamentary group. "Now we are trying to talk with other parties."
The Socialist Party held meetings with the other government parties all throughout Friday but no final statement on their stance to the election had been released.

The Socialists are part of a nine-party national unity government that was installed to stem the unrest. They and the others want more seats allocated on a proportional basis, while the Democratic Party wants more majority voting.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were deeply flawed.
Vranitzky, a special envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), earlier said he did not think the planned election date of June 29 should be postponed.
His spokeswoman said the OSCE still planned to prepare to monitor the elections, vital for them to be considered free and fair in international eyes.
"We hope they will come to some sort of solution very soon," the spokeswoman told journalists.
"We are ready for the monitoring and we just hope that all the political parties will be on board," she added.
Vranitzky again warned that the international community was closely watching Albania.
"Albanian politicians must be aware of the fact that the international community may reconsider its preparedness to offer assistance," he said.
Italy, leader of a multi-national military force to safeguard aid supplies to Albania, has said the troops may leave if the deal on early elections falls apart.
